summary: How did anyone ever think of that?

In October 1957 two young physicists in Maryland, listening to the beeps of Sputnik, worked out where the satellite was from the way its radio note rose and fell as it passed overhead. A colleague then turned the question round: if you already knew where the satellite was, could its signal tell you where *you* were? That question became the first satellite navigation system, and every phone that finds its way home is still answering it.

*A Connected History of Science and Technology* follows 3.3 million years of invention, from flaked stones in Kenya that may be the oldest tools ever found to samples brought back from the far side of the Moon. Its 951 entries cover medicine and mathematics, farming and physics, ships, engines, codes and computers, across every inhabited continent, and they are linked wherever one discovery truly passed something to another. Start anywhere, then follow an idea back to the people who made it possible, or forward to the strangers who used it in ways its inventors never imagined.

method: Each of the 11,854 citations leads to one of 3,166 works in the bibliography, so a reader can follow the evidence as far as curiosity takes them. Every factual claim in the book is recorded with the source that supports it and was read against that source before publication; where sources disagree or a date is uncertain, the entry says so.

The text was drafted and checked with AI tools, working from the cited sources, and edited by Ian Pitchford. It has not been peer reviewed. Links between entries are made only where a source documents that something passed from one to the other; a missing link is not a claim that two discoveries were independent.
